chapters.title: Creating Blue Oceans
chapters.sourcePressure: Establish the red-ocean versus blue-ocean contrast, the strategic move as the unit of analysis, and value innovation as the way to create new demand rather than fight over shrinking profit pools.
chapters.coreMove: Shift the strategic question from how to beat rivals to what value leap could make the old comparison less relevant.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating blue ocean strategy as a slogan for being creative, disruptive, or nicer than competitors.

chapters.title: Analytical Tools and Frameworks
chapters.sourcePressure: Turn the blue-ocean idea into visible tools: strategy canvas, value curve, four actions framework, and ERRC grid for challenging inherited industry factors.
chapters.coreMove: Make the industry value curve visible, then redesign it by eliminating, reducing, raising, and creating factors as one coherent move.
chapters.commonMisread: Using the tools as brainstorming worksheets that add features without changing the curve.

chapters.title: Reconstruct Market Boundaries
chapters.sourcePressure: Use the six paths framework to minimize search risk by looking across alternatives, strategic groups, buyer groups, complements, functional-emotional orientation, and time.
chapters.coreMove: Look across one accepted market boundary until a different buyer, alternative, complement, emotion, or trend changes the search field.
chapters.commonMisread: Thinking reconstruction means making a wild leap outside the business instead of systematically looking across known borders.

chapters.title: Focus on the Big Picture, Not the Numbers
chapters.sourcePressure: Keep strategy grounded in whole-pattern visual judgment, using the strategy canvas to see strategic sameness and possible divergence instead of drowning in isolated metrics.
chapters.coreMove: Step back from local metrics and force the whole value pattern into view before deciding what the numbers mean.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the chapter as anti-data or as permission to ignore financial discipline.

chapters.title: Reach Beyond Existing Demand
chapters.sourcePressure: Move beyond serving current customers by examining the three tiers of noncustomers: soon-to-be, refusing, and unexplored outsiders who reveal common barriers to demand.
chapters.coreMove: Listen to the people near, against, and far outside the market until the common blocker to broader demand becomes visible.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating noncustomers as another target segment to market at with louder acquisition tactics.

chapters.title: Get the Strategic Sequence Right
chapters.sourcePressure: Test promising ideas in order: buyer utility, strategic price, target cost, and adoption, so novelty becomes commercially viable value innovation.
chapters.coreMove: Run a promising idea through utility, price, cost, and adoption in sequence before excitement turns it into a launch.
chapters.commonMisread: Assuming buyer enthusiasm or originality is enough to prove a blue-ocean move is ready.

chapters.title: Overcome Key Organizational Hurdles
chapters.sourcePressure: Apply tipping point leadership to execution hurdles by focusing leverage on cognitive, resource, motivational, and political barriers instead of trying to move everyone evenly.
chapters.coreMove: Find the few hotspots, direct experiences, kingpins, and blockers that can tip execution through organizational resistance.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating organizational change as a morale campaign where everyone needs equal persuasion and equal resources.

chapters.title: Build Execution into Strategy
chapters.sourcePressure: Use fair process: engagement, explanation, and expectation clarity, so execution commitment is built during strategy formation rather than demanded afterward.
chapters.coreMove: Earn cooperation by engaging people before the choice, explaining the reasoning after it, and making the new expectations unmistakable.
chapters.commonMisread: Thinking fair process means consensus, endless input, or making everyone happy with the final decision.

chapters.title: Align Value, Profit, and People Propositions
chapters.sourcePressure: Sustain a blue ocean by aligning the value proposition for buyers, profit proposition for the organization, and people proposition for those who must deliver or support it.
chapters.coreMove: Check whether the buyer promise, profit model, and people system reinforce each other before calling a strategy sustainable.
chapters.commonMisread: Mistaking a loved customer offer for a complete strategy when costs or people incentives cannot support it.

chapters.title: Renew Blue Oceans
chapters.sourcePressure: Use the pioneer-migrator-settler map as a portfolio view so leaders renew blue oceans before imitation turns current success into ordinary competition.
chapters.coreMove: Read the portfolio for settlers, migrators, and pioneers, then fund renewal before today's strong numbers hide tomorrow's weakness.
chapters.commonMisread: Assuming a successful blue ocean remains safe as long as revenue is still growing.

chapters.title: Avoid Red Ocean Traps
chapters.sourcePressure: Close by warning against relapse into red-ocean logic: benchmarking rivals, fighting over existing demand, technology-first moves, niche-only thinking, and imitation disguised as strategy.
chapters.coreMove: Spot when a strategic move has become competitor-first or existing-demand-first, then pull the question back to buyer value and new demand.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating red-ocean traps as a list of bad tactics rather than a mindset that turns useful tools into imitation.
